issues.legal_issue: A wife's sister's husband is not barred from adoption under the Goda Dattak custom merely by the orthodox restriction concerning prohibited-marriage relationships.
material_facts: A widow adopted her sister's husband under the Goda Dattak custom.
The challenger did not establish a Goda Dattak custom barring that adoption.
The court found that the orthodox rule invoked from the Dattaka Mimansa was recommendatory and that the adoptee was not shown to fall within the prohibited relationship described by that rule.
issues.conclusion: The adoptee's relationship to the widow did not make the adoption invalid.
issues.legal_principle: The Dattaka Mimansa's restriction concerning the son of a woman who could not be married because of a Viruddha Sambandha relationship is recommendatory, not mandatory, as held in Mst. Abhiraj Kuer v. Devendra Singh (C.A. No. 379 of 1958, decided September 15, 1961). The court further held that even if orthodox Dattak restrictions applied to Goda adoption, they did not bar adoption of a wife's sister's husband; no provision was relied on.

rule.if: customary_adoption_case and adoptee_is_widows_sisters_husband and not proven_custom_bars_that_relationship

predicates.customary_adoption_case: The dispute concerns the validity of an adoption made under a community's customary adoption practice.
predicates.adoptee_is_widows_sisters_husband: The widow adopted her sister's husband as a son to her deceased husband.
predicates.proven_custom_bars_that_relationship: Evidence establishes a custom in the relevant community that bars adopting a person in the adoptee's relationship to the widow.
predicates.adoption_not_invalid_due_to_adoptees_rel: The adoption is not invalid because of the adoptee's relationship to the widow.

issues.definition: When a customary-adoption dispute concerns a widow's adoption of her sister's husband and no custom barring that relationship is established, the adoption is not invalid on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A custom requiring an adoptee to come from the adoptive father's family whenever possible must be proved before it can invalidate a customary adoption made outside that family.
material_facts: The challenger alleged that a Goda Dattak adoptee had to come from the adoptive father's family if a suitable family member was available.
The challenger did not establish that custom through authoritative texts or the testimony of a knowledgeable witness.
There was evidence of adoptions from other families when members of the adoptive father's family were present.
issues.conclusion: The alleged family-preference custom was not proved and did not invalidate the adoption.
issues.legal_principle: A party relying on a custom that limits eligibility for customary adoption must establish that custom. The court found the evidence insufficient to establish the alleged Goda Dattak restriction; it relied on no particular statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: customary_adoption_challenge and alleged_family_preference_custom and not custom_proven_by_reliable_evidence

predicates.customary_adoption_challenge: A party challenges the validity of an adoption made under a community's customary practice.
predicates.alleged_family_preference_custom: The challenger asserts that an adoptee must come from the adoptive father's family when a member of that family is available.
predicates.custom_proven_by_reliable_evidence: Authoritative texts or reliable testimony establish the alleged family-preference custom.
predicates.adoption_not_invalid_due_to_family_prefe: The adoption is not invalid because the adoptee came from outside the adoptive father's family.

issues.definition: In a challenge based on an alleged family-preference custom, if reliable evidence does not establish that custom, the adoption is not invalid for choosing an adoptee from outside the adoptive father's family.

issues.legal_issue: A husband's expressed preference for a particular adoptee does not by itself establish an implied prohibition against adopting anyone else.
material_facts: A letter and witness evidence showed that the husband had authorized his widow to adopt and preferred a particular boy.
The letter did not indicate that no other person could be adopted.
The challenger's testimony that the husband had restricted adoption to the challenger or his sons was uncorroborated, and the other evidence did not establish such a restriction.
issues.conclusion: No implied prohibition against adopting anyone other than the preferred boy or the challenger's family members was proved.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the husband's statements and the evidence as a whole, distinguishing authorization and preference from an intention to prohibit all other adoptions. It relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: customary_adoption_challenge and husband_authorized_adoption and husband_expressed_preference and not evidence_proves_exclusive_adoption_direction

predicates.customary_adoption_challenge: A party challenges the validity of an adoption made under a community's customary practice.
predicates.husband_authorized_adoption: Before his death, the husband authorized his widow to make an adoption after his death.
predicates.husband_expressed_preference: The husband expressed a preference for a particular prospective adoptee.
predicates.evidence_proves_exclusive_adoption_direc: Reliable evidence establishes that the husband directed that only the preferred person or a specified class of people could be adopted.
predicates.no_implied_prohibition_established: An implied prohibition against adopting other people is not established.

issues.definition: When a husband authorized an adoption and expressed a preference, but reliable evidence does not establish that he restricted adoption exclusively to that preference, no implied prohibition is established.

issues.legal_issue: A widow does not need the consent of her husband's sapindas for an adoption where her husband authorized her to adopt.
material_facts: The widow's husband had authorized her during his lifetime to make an adoption after his death.
The letter and the challenger's witnesses supported the finding of authorization, although the husband had also expressed a preference for a particular boy.
The challenger argued that consent of the husband's sapindas was required if the parties were governed by the Madras School of Mitakshara.
issues.conclusion: The absence of sapinda consent did not invalidate the adoption because the husband had authorized it.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Madras School of Mitakshara rule invoked by the challenger, consent of the husband's sapindas is necessary only where the husband has not authorized the widow to adopt. The court therefore found it unnecessary to decide whether that rule otherwise applied or whether the amendment application had been properly rejected; it cited no earlier case for this issue.

predicates.widow_adoption_case: The proceeding concerns the validity of an adoption made by a widow after her husband's death.
predicates.husband_authorized_adoption: Before his death, the husband authorized his widow to make an adoption after his death.
predicates.sapinda_consent_not_required: The adoption does not require the consent of the husband's sapindas.

issues.definition: In a widow's adoption case, if the husband authorized the adoption, sapinda consent is not required.
